question: What is the most accurate speech-to-text API?
answer:
There's no single winner. The most accurate API depends on your audio, language, and whether you need streaming. Here's what the search turned up. Most of it comes from vendors or affiliated blogs, so treat it with caution.

- **Voice-agent benchmark:** A Coval benchmark of five APIs ran 2,400 runs per model. It put Gradium STT first at 2.4% WER. Deepgram Nova 3 and Nova 2 were fastest but had the highest WER, around 25%. Gradium is one of the vendors tested and published the article, so it has a stake in the result. ([Gradium](https://gradium.ai/content/stt-api-benchmark-2026-latency-accuracy))
- **Batch transcription on real-world audio:** One May 2026 guide lists Deepgram Nova-3 as its best hosted pick, at 5.26% WER across 9 audio domains. It says NVIDIA Canary Qwen 2.5B leads the open-source models on the Open ASR Leaderboard, at 5.63%. ([Future AGI](https://futureagi.com/blog/speech-to-text-apis-in-2026-benchmarks-pricing-developer-s-decision-guide))
- **Speechmatics:** One page calls it the accuracy leader, citing 6.4% aggregate WER for its Melia-1 model. The figures are largely vendor-reported. ([VexaScribe](https://vexascribe.com/how-accurate-is-speechmatics))
- **Independent index:** Artificial Analysis publishes an AA-WER index. It averages WER, weighted by audio duration, over about 8 hours from three datasets. It's probably the most neutral place to compare current models. ([Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text/models/llm-speech))

Accuracy also varies a lot with conditions. A model with 3% WER on clean podcasts can reach 15% on noisy call-center audio.

I'd shortlist two or three of Deepgram Nova-3, Speechmatics, AssemblyAI, and the top models on Artificial Analysis. Then run 30–60 minutes of your own representative audio through each and compare WER. If you tell me your use case (real-time or batch, languages, noise level), I can narrow the list.

Sources:
- [STT API Benchmark 2026 (Gradium)](https://gradium.ai/content/stt-api-benchmark-2026-latency-accuracy)
- [Speech-to-Text APIs in 2026 (Future AGI)](https://futureagi.com/blog/speech-to-text-apis-in-2026-benchmarks-pricing-developer-s-decision-guide)
- [How accurate is Speechmatics (VexaScribe)](https://vexascribe.com/how-accurate-is-speechmatics)
- [Artificial Analysis – Speech to Text](https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text/models/llm-speech)

Vendor WER numbers are usually measured on clean audio, so they can differ sharply from production results.

Bottom line: the top spot depends on the benchmark, and vendor-sourced numbers are not directly comparable. For a decision, the best approach is to run a shared test set of your own audio through the candidate APIs.

question: What is the best real-time streaming speech recognition API for voice agents?
answer:
**There's no single best API. For most voice agents, start with Deepgram (Nova-3 or Flux).** Then test one or two alternatives on your own audio.

**Top options**
- **Deepgram (Nova-3 / Flux):** This is the most consistent pick for agents where turn timing matters. Sources report streaming latency under 300ms. They also say Flux, which has built-in end-of-turn detection, has median end-of-turn detection under 300ms. It also supports on-prem deployment for regulated industries. ([futureagi](https://futureagi.com/blog/speech-to-text-apis-in-2026-benchmarks-pricing-developer-s-decision-guide/), [Coval](https://www.coval.ai/blog/best-speech-to-text-providers-in-2026-independent-benchmarks-and-how-to-choose/), [Deepgram](https://deepgram.com/learn/deepgram-vs-assemblyai-vs-whisper))
- **AssemblyAI (Universal-3 Pro Streaming):** It's a good choice if you want audio intelligence features and tunable latency modes. Its latency figures vary a lot by source: about 150ms P50 in one, about 300ms in another, and about 760ms time-to-final in a third. That spread is a reason to test it yourself. ([Inworld](https://inworld.ai/resources/best-voice-to-text-api), [Gladia](https://www.gladia.io/blog/assemblyai-vs-deepgram), [futureagi](https://futureagi.com/blog/speech-to-text-apis-in-2026-benchmarks-pricing-developer-s-decision-guide/))
- **ElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime:** It's reported at roughly 150ms to the first partial transcript, with strong multilingual coverage. It's worth testing if your agent is multilingual. ([futureagi](https://futureagi.com/blog/speech-to-text-apis-in-2026-benchmarks-pricing-developer-s-decision-guide/))
- **Gladia (Solaria-1):** It's reported at about 103ms for partial transcripts and 270ms for final ones. ([Gladia](https://www.gladia.io/blog/best-speech-to-text-apis))
- **Speechmatics:** It's noted for accent-heavy and multilingual speech, but it publishes no streaming latency figure. ([DIY AI](https://diyai.io/ai-tools/speech-to-text/best-real-time-speech-to-text-apis/))

**Caveats**
- Most of these numbers are vendor claims or come from vendor-adjacent blogs. Gladia and Deepgram, for example, publish comparisons that include their own products.
- Transcription speed isn't the only factor in how fast an agent responds. Endpointing (deciding when the user has finished speaking), interruption handling, and network distance often matter as much.

**How to pick**
1. Shortlist Deepgram plus one or two others, based on your languages and compliance needs.
2. Test them on your own audio, with your accents, background noise, phone-quality codecs, and domain vocabulary.
3. Measure word error rate, time to final transcript, and how often the agent cuts users off or waits too long.

question: What is the best real-time streaming speech recognition API for voice agents?
answer:
**There's no single best option. For most voice agents, start with Deepgram (Flux), and compare it against AssemblyAI.** I got this from vendor blogs and comparison pages, not independent benchmarks, so treat the numbers as rough.

**Top choices**
- **Deepgram Flux:** It's the most consistently recommended for voice agents. It has built-in end-of-turn detection, so you don't need a separate voice activity detection (VAD) step. Deepgram claims a median end-of-turn time under 300ms, which it says saves 200–600ms of agent response time compared with a separate STT and VAD pipeline. A multilingual version was announced in April 2026.
- **AssemblyAI Universal-3 Pro Streaming:** This is the main alternative. One source reports about 150ms P50 latency, but another comparison shows a much larger gap, so the sources conflict. It lets you tune the trade-off between latency and accuracy. Reported pricing is about $0.45/hour for the flagship realtime tier and $0.15/hour for the cheaper Universal-Streaming tier.
- **ElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime:** It's reported at under 150ms transcription latency over WebSocket. It's worth testing, especially if you already use ElevenLabs for text-to-speech.
- **Gladia Solaria:** It's another low-latency option. It's mentioned mainly in Gladia's own comparison pages, so the figures come from the vendor.

**Choosing between them**
- **Turn-taking and interruptions:** Deepgram Flux.
- **Tunable latency and accuracy, or extra transcript features:** AssemblyAI.
- **Multilingual or code-switching audio:** Test Flux Multilingual, Gladia and ElevenLabs on your own languages.
- **Cost at scale:** Compare per-hour streaming prices, because they vary a lot between tiers.

**Before you commit**
- Several pages I found are stale. One still cites Deepgram's older Nova-2 model.
- Test your top two or three on your own audio. Use your real accents, phone-quality audio, noise and domain vocabulary.
- Measure time to first partial transcript, time to final transcript, end-of-turn accuracy, and word error rate.
- Measure over your actual network path, because that changes the latency.

question: What should I use instead of self-hosting Whisper?
answer:
Here are the main alternatives to self-hosting Whisper. This is from my own knowledge, and I haven't checked current pricing or model lineups. Both change often.

**Hosted Whisper / OpenAI**
- **OpenAI Audio API**: This is the simplest swap. It offers `whisper-1` and the newer `gpt-4o-transcribe` and `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` models, which are generally more accurate.
- **Groq**: It hosts Whisper large-v3 and turbo and is very fast and cheap. It's a good drop-in option if you want to keep Whisper behavior.
- **Fireworks, Together, Replicate, Fal, Deepgram-hosted Whisper**: These host Whisper with pay-per-use pricing.

**Dedicated speech-to-text APIs**
- **Deepgram (Nova)**: Low latency, strong streaming, and good pricing. It's a good choice for real-time use.
- **AssemblyAI**: Strong accuracy, plus built-in diarization, summarization, and other audio features.
- **Google Cloud Speech-to-Text (Chirp)**, **Azure Speech**, and **AWS Transcribe**: These make sense if you're already on one of those clouds or need compliance features.
- **ElevenLabs Scribe**: Very accurate, with good multilingual support and diarization.
- **Speechmatics**: Strong on accents and many languages.
- **Gladia**: A Whisper-based API with extra features.

**Choosing**
- **Simplest and cheapest, with Whisper-like output:** Groq.
- **Real-time or streaming:** Deepgram, or AssemblyAI.
- **Speaker labels and audio intelligence:** AssemblyAI, or ElevenLabs Scribe.
- **Highest accuracy on hard audio:** Benchmark `gpt-4o-transcribe`, Scribe, and Deepgram on your own samples.
- **Privacy or compliance:** Azure, AWS, or Google, or a vendor that offers a zero-retention or BAA agreement.
- **Mostly local, low-effort use:** If you only need it on-device, such as on a Mac, skip the server and use whisper.cpp, MLX-Whisper, or a desktop app like MacWhisper.

Tell me your use case (batch or real-time, languages, volume, privacy needs). I can narrow this down and look up current pricing and benchmarks.

question: Which speech-to-text APIs support PII redaction for healthcare or finance?
answer:
These are the main options as of my last knowledge. Features and compliance terms change often, so check each vendor's current docs before you commit.

**Built-in PII redaction in the transcription API**

| Provider | PII feature | Compliance notes |
|---|---|---|
| **AssemblyAI** | PII redaction in text, and audio redaction that beeps out the spoken PII. It has configurable policies such as `medical_condition`, `drug`, `blood_type`, `credit_card_number`, `banking_information`, `ssn`, and `injury`. | Offers a HIPAA BAA. SOC 2. |
| **Deepgram** | `redact` parameter with options like `pci`, `pii`, `numbers`, and newer entity-based redaction. | Offers a BAA on enterprise plans. SOC 2. PCI-oriented redaction suits finance. |
| **AWS Transcribe** | Standard Transcribe has content redaction for PII. **Transcribe Call Analytics** has redaction too. **Amazon Transcribe Medical** is a separate service for clinical speech, and it identifies PHI. | HIPAA-eligible under an AWS BAA. PCI DSS and SOC. |
| **Google Cloud Speech-to-Text** | No full PII redaction in the API. The usual approach is to pair it with **Cloud DLP / Sensitive Data Protection** to de-identify transcripts. | HIPAA support under a BAA. |
| **Azure AI Speech** | Transcription itself doesn't redact. Pair it with **Azure AI Language PII detection**. It has a dedicated PHI detection mode, and the Language service can redact conversational PII. | HIPAA via BAA. Broad compliance coverage. |
| **Speechmatics** | Offers some entity and redaction-style options, but check current docs. | Offers on-prem and private deployment. |
| **Rev AI / Verbit / Otter-style tools** | Redaction is limited or handled through enterprise workflows. | Confirm with the vendor. |

**Healthcare-specific vendors**
- **Amazon Transcribe Medical** and **Nuance DAX / Dragon Medical** are for clinical documentation. Nuance's tools are part of Microsoft.
- **Suki, Abridge, and Deepgram's medical models** are ambient or clinical-focused options.

**Finance-specific notes**
- Deepgram's `pci` option and AssemblyAI's `credit_card_number` and `banking_information` policies both target card and account data.
- AWS Transcribe Call Analytics is common in contact centers, where PCI compliance matters.
- For PCI, check whether redaction happens *before* the transcript is stored or returned. Also check whether the audio itself can be redacted.

**What to check before choosing**
1. **A signed BAA** (HIPAA) or PCI attestation. A feature alone doesn't make you compliant.
2. **Audio redaction versus text-only redaction.** Many APIs redact only the transcript.
3. **Recall on entities.** Test with your own audio, because missed PII is the main risk. Accents and numbers read aloud are common failure points.
4. **Data retention and training policies.** Make sure the vendor doesn't keep or train on your data.
5. **Deployment options.** Self-hosted or VPC options matter for strict requirements.

**Open-source approach:** You can transcribe with Whisper locally, then run **Microsoft Presidio** or a similar NER-based redactor on the text. This keeps data in-house, but you own the compliance burden.

I can search for the latest pricing and features for any of these, or compare two or three in more depth. Which use case are you building for: call recordings, clinical dictation, or something else?

answer:
Several major speech-to-text APIs offer PII redaction. This comes from my own knowledge, not a fresh search, so check each vendor's current docs before you commit.

## Dedicated STT vendors

| Provider | PII redaction | Healthcare/finance notes |
|---|---|---|
| **AssemblyAI** | Redacts PII in the transcript text, and can produce redacted audio. Policies cover categories such as medical conditions, drugs, banking details, credit cards, SSNs, and DOB. | Offers a HIPAA BAA. |
| **Deepgram** | The `redact` parameter covers PCI, PII, and numbers, and works on both pre-recorded and streaming audio. | Offers a BAA, plus on-prem or VPC deployment. |
| **Speechmatics** | Offers some entity-based redaction and masking. | Supports on-prem deployment. Check how complete its PII coverage is. |
| **Rev AI** | Offers profanity filtering and some redaction options. | Check the docs for the current PII scope. |
| **Gladia** | Offers PII-related options for audio intelligence. | Verify the specifics. |

## Cloud providers

- **AWS Transcribe** has content redaction for PII in standard transcription. **Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics** also supports redaction. **AWS Transcribe Medical** covers clinical dictation and conversations, and AWS signs a BAA for HIPAA-eligible services.
- **Google Cloud Speech-to-Text** has no built-in PII redaction. The usual pattern is to pair it with **Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Sensitive Data Protection)** to redact the transcript. Google also offers a medical-specific model.
- **Azure AI Speech** can be combined with the **Azure AI Language PII detection** feature, which has a conversational PII mode for call transcripts. Azure also offers a BAA.

## Specialized healthcare options

- **Nuance DAX / Dragon Medical** is clinical-grade, though it's an ambient documentation product more than a plain API.
- **Amazon HealthScribe** is a HIPAA-eligible clinical documentation service with sensitive-data handling.
- **Suki, Abridge, and similar vendors** offer scribe-style products, some with APIs.

## Finance and contact center

For PCI-style redaction, such as card numbers read aloud on calls, look at:
- **Deepgram** (PCI redaction option)
- **AWS Transcribe Call Analytics**
- **AssemblyAI**
- **Twilio** or **Amazon Connect** pipelines, which can pause recording or redact during payment capture

## Things to check

1. **Audio vs. text redaction.** Some vendors redact only the transcript, while the original audio is still stored. Check retention and deletion policies.
2. **Streaming vs. batch support.** Redaction features often differ between the two.
3. **Accuracy.** Spoken numbers, names, and accents cause misses. Test on your own data and measure recall, since a missed PII item is the costly error.
4. **Compliance paperwork.** Confirm that a BAA (HIPAA), SOC 2, PCI DSS attestation, and data residency options are available.
5. **Defense in depth.** Many teams add a second redaction pass on the transcript with a tool like Microsoft Presidio, Google DLP, or AWS Comprehend Medical.

question: What should I use instead of self-hosting Whisper?
answer:
The right choice depends on what you need. These are the main managed options.

**Hosted Whisper APIs (easiest swap)**
- **OpenAI Audio API** (`whisper-1`, `gpt-4o-transcribe`, `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe`): the least code to change if you already use Whisper. The newer gpt-4o models are generally more accurate.
- **Groq**: hosts Whisper large-v3 and turbo. It's very fast and cheap, and the API is OpenAI-compatible.
- **Fireworks, Together, Replicate, Deepgram-hosted Whisper**: other hosts of the same open model, useful if you want to compare price and latency.

**Dedicated speech-to-text vendors (often better for production)**
- **Deepgram (Nova)**: low latency, strong streaming, and good pricing.
- **AssemblyAI**: strong accuracy, plus built-in diarization, summarization, and PII redaction.
- **Google Cloud Speech-to-Text (Chirp)**, **Azure Speech**, and **AWS Transcribe**: a good fit if you're already in one of those clouds or have compliance needs.
- **ElevenLabs Scribe**: high accuracy across many languages.
- **Speechmatics**: strong on accents and multilingual audio.

**How to choose**
- **Real-time or streaming:** Deepgram, AssemblyAI, or Google. Whisper isn't designed for streaming.
- **Cheapest batch transcription:** Groq or another hosted Whisper.
- **Speaker labels and extras:** AssemblyAI or Deepgram.
- **Strict privacy or compliance:** Azure, AWS, or Google with a BAA or data residency. Otherwise, self-hosting may be justified after all.
- **Minimal code changes:** OpenAI or Groq.

Pricing and model rankings change often, and I haven't checked current numbers. If you tell me your use case (language, batch or streaming, audio volume, budget), I can narrow it to one or two options and look up current pricing.

question: AssemblyAI vs Deepgram
answer:
**Short version:** AssemblyAI is usually the pick for batch transcription with built-in "audio intelligence" features. Deepgram is usually the pick for low-latency streaming and voice agents. Most of the sources below are vendor-written or aggregators, so treat the numbers as rough.

| | AssemblyAI | Deepgram |
|---|---|---|
| **Best for** | Batch transcription, plus summarization, sentiment, PII redaction and similar features | Real-time streaming and voice agents |
| **Latency** | Competitive, but described as generally slower in streaming | Reported at under 300 ms streaming |
| **Accuracy** | One guide gives it the edge on accuracy and compliance features | Its own page claims 30% lower WER than AssemblyAI; no basis is shown |
| **Pricing** | From about $0.15/hr, with a $50 free credit | Nova-3 from about $0.0077/min (about $0.46/hr), with a $200 free credit |
| **Voice agent API** | About $4.50/hr, flat rate | About $4.50/hr, tiered plus concurrency charges |

- **Accuracy:** The sources disagree. One third-party review calls the two roughly equal, even in noisy audio.
- **Pricing:** The sources conflict here too, and some claim Deepgram is far cheaper. Add-ons such as diarization and summarization are often billed separately, so base rates understate the real cost.
- **Recommendation:** Run both on a sample of your own audio and compare WER, latency and total cost, including add-ons. Check each vendor's pricing page first, since rates change often.

question: AssemblyAI vs OpenAI Whisper for transcription
answer:
**AssemblyAI vs. OpenAI Whisper**

Most of the numbers below come from vendor or aggregator sites and they conflict with each other. Treat them as rough guidance.

| | AssemblyAI | Whisper |
|---|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | AssemblyAI's own page claims about 4.1% WER on CommonVoice English versus 8.5% for Whisper. It also claims 10.0% versus 11.6% on noisy English audio. | Good general accuracy, with 99-language coverage. It can hallucinate on silence or noise. |
| **Extra features** | Speaker diarization, PII redaction, summarization, sentiment analysis, and real-time streaming are built in. | Mostly just transcription. The vendor page says diarization and streaming aren't native. You add them yourself. |
| **Pricing** | Reported anywhere from about $0.002 to $0.0035 per minute, depending on the source and tier. | The OpenAI API is about $0.003 per minute. Groq-hosted Whisper is much cheaper, about $0.04 to $0.11 per hour. |
| **Hosting** | Managed API only. | Open weights, so you can self-host. That means you run the GPU, queue, and reliability. |

**Choose AssemblyAI if:**
- You want production-ready features without building them yourself, such as diarization, redaction, and live streaming.
- You work with noisy or difficult audio and need compliance features.

**Choose Whisper if:**
- Cost is the priority, especially at high volume through Groq or self-hosting.
- You need data to stay on your own infrastructure.
- You need wide language coverage.
- You're happy to build the surrounding pipeline.

The accuracy claims come from AssemblyAI's own benchmarks, not neutral testing. Run both on 20–30 minutes of your own audio and compare WER. Also check the current pricing pages before you commit.

**AssemblyAI vs. OpenAI Whisper**

Most of the numbers below come from vendor or aggregator sites and they conflict with each other. Treat them as rough guidance.

| | AssemblyAI | Whisper |
|---|---|---|

**Choose AssemblyAI if:**
- You want production-ready features without building them yourself, such as diarization, redaction, and live streaming.
- You work with noisy or difficult audio and need compliance features.

**Choose Whisper if:**
- Cost is the priority, especially at high volume through Groq or self-hosting.
- You need data to stay on your own infrastructure.
- You need wide language coverage.
- You're happy to build the surrounding pipeline.

The accuracy claims come from AssemblyAI's own benchmarks, not neutral testing. Run both on 20–30 minutes of your own audio and compare WER. Also check the current pricing pages before you commit.

question: How much does Fireworks AI cost?
answer:
Fireworks AI is pay-as-you-go, and the price depends on how you use it. These figures come from their pricing page as of today.

**Serverless inference**
- You pay per token (input, output and cached) from prepaid credits.
- Rates vary by model, and the pricing page doesn't list them. Check the model library or pricing docs for a specific model.
- Embeddings cost $0.008 per 1M input tokens for models up to 150M parameters and $0.016 for 150M–350M. Qwen3 8B is $0.10 per 1M, which they call a limited-time offer.
- You can set a monthly spend limit and turn on auto-reload.

**On-demand GPUs** (billed per second)

| GPU | Per hour |
|---|---|
| H100 80GB | $8.00 |
| H200 141GB | $8.00 |
| B200 180GB | $13.00 |
| B300 288GB | $15.00 |
| GB300 288GB | $20.00 |

Region-restricted deployments cost 1.5x.

**Fine-tuning** (per 1M training tokens)

| Base model size | LoRA SFT | LoRA DPO | Full SFT | Full DPO |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Up to 16B | $0.50 | $1.00 | $1.00 | $2.00 |
| 16.1B–80B | $3.00 | $6.00 | $6.00 | $12.00 |
| 80B–300B | $6.00 | $12.00 | $12.00 | $24.00 |
| Over 300B | $10.00 | $20.00 | $20.00 | $40.00 |

- Fine-tuned models are served at the same price as the base model.
- The serverless Training API has no idle cost. Its training rates range from about $4.10 to $32.55 per 1M tokens, depending on the model.

**Enterprise:** Pricing is by contact with sales.

**Free credits:** The page lists no general free credits. Muse Glimmer 30B SFT fine-tuning is free until 11/30.

Source: https://fireworks.ai/pricing

content.content:
## Fireworks AI Pricing Summary

**Serverless Inference**
- Pay per token from prepaid credits. Usage is billed on input, output, and cached tokens.
- Auto Reload tops up your balance, and a monthly spend limit caps usage.
- Per-token rates for popular models are in the full pricing docs, not on this page. The page mentions Standard, Priority, and Fast serving paths.
- Embeddings: $0.008 per 1M input tokens (up to 150M parameters), $0.016 (150M–350M), and $0.10 for Qwen3 8B (limited-time offer).

**Image Models**
- This page does not list image model pricing.

**Fine-Tuning (per 1M training tokens)**

| Base model size | LoRA SFT | LoRA DPO | Full SFT | Full DPO |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Up to 16B | $0.50 | $1.00 | $1.00 | $2.00 |
| 16.1B–80B | $3.00 | $6.00 | $6.00 | $12.00 |
| 80B–300B | $6.00 | $12.00 | $12.00 | $24.00 |
| Over 300B | $10.00 | $20.00 | $20.00 | $40.00 |

- Fine-tuned models are served at the same price as base models.
- Serverless Training API: pay per token prefilled, sampled, and trained, with no idle cost. Train rates range from about $4.10 (Qwen 3.8 27B) to $32.55 (Kimi K3) per 1M tokens.

**On-Demand GPU Rates**

| GPU | Per hour | Per minute |
|---|---|---|
| H100 80GB | $8.00 | $0.134 |
| H200 141GB | $8.00 | $0.134 |
| B200 180GB | $13.00 | $0.217 |
| B300 288GB | $15.00 | $0.250 |
| GB300 288GB | $20.00 | $0.334 |

- Billed per GPU second with no extra startup charges.
- Region-restricted deployments cost a 1.5x premium.

**Tiers**
- **Serverless:** self-serve, pay as you go.
- **On-Demand:** pay per GPU second, for higher rate limits and lower costs at scale.
- **Enterprise:** contact sales for faster speeds, lower costs, and higher rate limits.

**Free Credits**
- No general free credit offer is listed.
- Muse Glimmer 30B SFT is free through the UI and Serverless Training API until 11/30, with no credit card required.

question: AssemblyAI vs OpenAI Whisper for transcription
answer:
**Short version:** AssemblyAI is a managed API with a lot of built-in features. Whisper is cheap and flexible, but you have to build more yourself.

| | AssemblyAI | OpenAI Whisper |
|---|---|---|
| **Form** | Hosted API only | Open-source model you can self-host, or OpenAI's hosted API |
| **Accuracy** | Generally rated higher on English and hard audio | Strong, especially for multilingual audio. It can hallucinate text during silence or noise. |
| **Built-in features** | Speaker diarization, word-level timestamps, summaries, sentiment, PII redaction, topic detection, LLM-based audio analysis | Basic transcription and translation. You have to add diarization and the rest yourself. |
| **Streaming** | Real-time streaming API | Not native. You need workarounds or other tooling. |
| **Languages** | Many, but fewer than Whisper | About 99 |
| **Cost** | Roughly $0.15–$0.21/hour, depending on the source | Hosted API about $0.36/hour. Third-party hosts like Groq are about $0.11/hour. Self-hosting costs only GPU time. |
| **Privacy/compliance** | Enterprise compliance offerings | Self-hosting keeps audio fully in-house |

**Choose AssemblyAI if** you want production-ready output quickly. That means speaker labels, real-time transcription, redaction, or analytics, with no infrastructure to run.

**Choose Whisper if** you need a wide range of languages, want audio to stay on your own hardware, are transcribing very large volumes where GPU costs beat per-minute fees, or want to fine-tune the model.

**Caveats:**
- The sources I found were mostly third-party blogs, and their pricing figures conflict. Check both vendors' pricing pages before deciding.
- I found no head-to-head benchmark. Test both on a sample of your own audio and compare word error rate. Accents, noise, and domain terms can change the result.

If you tell me your use case (language, volume, real-time or batch, privacy needs), I can give a more specific recommendation.

Sources:
- [AssemblyAI vs Whisper (OpenAI) — Pricing (2026)](https://costbench.com/compare/assemblyai-vs-openai-whisper/)
- [AI Transcription Pricing 2026: Whisper vs Deepgram vs AssemblyAI](https://dev.to/eli_9c82b7dfe52c1bc371ffe/ai-transcription-pricing-2026-whisper-vs-deepgram-vs-assemblyai-2eec)
- [Whisper vs AssemblyAI: Best Speech-to-Text API (Eden AI)](https://www.edenai.co/post/whisper-vs-assemblyai-best-speech-to-text-api)
- [G2: AssemblyAI vs OpenAI Whisper](https://www.g2.com/compare/assemblyai-speech-to-text-api-vs-openai-whisper)

question: What are the best AssemblyAI alternatives?
answer:
These are the main AssemblyAI alternatives, grouped by what they're best at. This comes from my own knowledge, not a fresh search, so check current pricing and model versions before you commit.

**Hosted speech-to-text APIs**
- **Deepgram** is the usual pick for low-latency streaming and real-time voice agents. Its Nova models are fast and cheap, and it supports custom model training.
- **OpenAI (Whisper and the gpt-4o-transcribe models)** is simple and accurate across many languages. It's weaker on real-time streaming, diarization, and extras like PII redaction.
- **Google Cloud Speech-to-Text (Chirp)** covers many languages and fits well if you already use GCP.
- **AWS Transcribe** integrates well with the AWS ecosystem. It has medical and call-analytics variants, and its accuracy is typically middling.
- **Azure AI Speech** is strong for enterprise needs, custom models, and compliance.
- **Speechmatics** is strong on accents, multilingual audio, and real-time use. It also offers on-prem deployment.
- **Gladia** is a Whisper-based API with diarization and a developer-friendly interface.
- **ElevenLabs (Scribe)** is a newer, high-accuracy option with good multilingual support.
- **Rev AI** is solid for English and can be paired with human transcription.

**Self-hosted or open source**
- **Whisper**, **faster-whisper**, or **WhisperX** (which adds alignment and diarization) give you full control and no per-minute fees. You pay in GPU and engineering time.
- **NVIDIA NeMo (Parakeet and Canary)** ranks near the top on open leaderboards and is very fast.
- **Vosk** and **Kaldi** are lightweight, but older and less accurate.

**Which to choose**
- **Real-time voice agents:** Deepgram, Speechmatics, or AssemblyAI's own streaming models.
- **Lowest cost at scale:** self-hosted Parakeet or faster-whisper, or Deepgram.
- **Multilingual accuracy:** Google Chirp, Speechmatics, ElevenLabs, or Whisper.
- **Compliance or enterprise needs:** Azure, AWS, or Google.
- **Audio intelligence features** (summaries, sentiment, PII redaction, topic detection): AssemblyAI is strong here. Deepgram and Speechmatics have some of these, but with other vendors you may need to add an LLM step.

Accuracy depends heavily on your audio, such as noise, accents, and domain vocabulary. I'd test 2–3 candidates on your own samples and compare word error rate, latency, and cost.

If you tell me your use case (real-time or batch, languages, volume, budget), I can narrow this down. I can also search for current benchmarks and pricing.

question: How much does AssemblyAI cost per hour of audio?
answer:
AssemblyAI's pricing page lists these base rates per hour of audio:

**Pre-recorded**
- Universal-3.5 Pro: **$0.21/hr**
- Universal-2: **$0.15/hr**
- Nano: $0.15/hr. It's deprecated and now routes to Universal-2.

**Streaming** (billed on WebSocket session time, so idle connection time counts)
- Universal-Streaming (English or Multilingual): **$0.15/hr**
- Universal-3.6 Pro Realtime: **$0.45/hr**

**Add-ons (charged on top of the base rate)**
- Speaker diarization: +$0.02/hr for standard async, +$0.065/hr for experimental async, and +$0.12/hr for streaming.
- Keyterms prompting: +$0.05/hr on async models, and +$0.04/hr on Universal-Streaming English. It's included on the other streaming models.
- Medical Mode: +$0.15/hr.
- General prompting (beta): +$0.05/hr.
- Voice Focus: +$0.10/hr, on Universal-3.6 Pro Realtime only.

For example, Universal-3.5 Pro with Medical Mode and standard diarization comes to $0.21 + $0.15 + $0.02 = $0.38/hr.

Speech Understanding and Guardrails add-ons are priced separately. I didn't get their rates. Check the pricing page for those, and for any volume discounts.

Sources: https://www.assemblyai.com/pricing

question: What are the best AssemblyAI alternatives?
answer:
The search results were mostly vendor blogs and directory sites, so the rankings may be biased. I added a few well-known options from my own knowledge, and those aren't from the search.

**Top API-level alternatives**
- **Deepgram** is built for developers. It's known for low-latency streaming, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice-agent tooling. It's a common pick for real-time and call-center use.
- **Speechmatics** is the enterprise option the sources mention most often. It supports 55+ languages and real-time use. It also offers on-prem deployment, which AssemblyAI doesn't (it's cloud-only).
- **OpenAI Whisper and GPT-4o Transcribe** are cheap and accurate. Whisper can be self-hosted. You'll have to add diarization, streaming, and other extras yourself.

**From my own knowledge (not in the search)**
- **Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, AWS Transcribe, and Azure Speech** make sense if you already use one of those clouds. They offer broad language coverage and compliance options, but they're often less accurate or less feature-rich than the specialists.
- **Gladia, Rev AI, and ElevenLabs Scribe** are other specialist APIs. I'd check current benchmarks and pricing for them.

**Other options from the search**
- **Puter.js** is a front end over several providers, including Whisper and GPT-4o Transcribe. Each end user covers their own transcription costs. That suits consumer apps better than business ones.
- **VRFY** is listed for regulated environments.
- **Wispr Flow** appeared in one list, but it's a consumer dictation app and not a substitute for an API.

**How to choose**
- **Real-time or voice agents:** Deepgram.
- **On-prem or data-residency needs:** Speechmatics, or self-hosted Whisper.
- **Lowest cost:** Whisper or GPT-4o Transcribe.
- **Already on a major cloud:** that cloud's native service.

None of the sources gave verified 2026 pricing. Test two or three candidates on your own audio and check current prices before you commit. Accuracy varies a lot by accent, noise, and domain.

# AssemblyAI vs Deepgram

Most of the comparison pages I found were written by one of the two vendors, so treat the claims about each other as biased. Deepgram's pricing page is the one first-party source I checked directly.

## Short version
- **Deepgram** is better for real-time and voice-agent work, for high volume, and when cost or latency matters most.
- **AssemblyAI** is better for batch transcription where you also want built-in "audio intelligence" (summaries, PII redaction, sentiment, and similar). It is also the one to look at if accuracy on named entities or compliance matters most.

## Comparison

| | Deepgram | AssemblyAI |
|---|---|---|
| **Streaming latency** | Usually described as faster, with claims of sub-300ms | Slightly slower in raw streaming latency, per a third-party review |
| **Core accuracy** | Roughly on par | Roughly on par. AssemblyAI claims an edge on real-world entities, but that claim is self-serving. |
| **Pricing (verified)** | Nova-3 pre-recorded is $0.26/hr pay-as-you-go. Streaming is $0.29/hr for Nova-3 and $0.39/hr for Flux. | I didn't verify this on their pricing page. Aggregators list $0.15–$0.37/hr. |
| **Add-ons** | Charged separately, such as redaction at $0.12/hr and diarization on streaming at $0.12/hr | Many intelligence features are built into the API |
| **Free credit** | $200, and it doesn't expire | Not verified |
| **Voice agents** | Nova-3 and Flux ("conversational" model), with tiered pricing plus concurrency charges | Flat $4.50/hr for the full STT + LLM + TTS pipeline, according to AssemblyAI |
| **Strengths** | Real-time speed, deployment flexibility, free tier | Intelligence features, compliance |

The pricing sources disagree. Deepgram says it is 2.5–3× cheaper, while an aggregator says 97% cheaper. At list price the gap looks much smaller than the aggregator claims. Add-ons and concurrency charges can also change the total.

## Recommendation
Run both on a sample of your own audio and measure word error rate, latency, and total cost including add-ons. The vendor benchmarks don't settle it.

question: Is AssemblyAI good for extracting insights and summaries from customer calls?
answer:
Yes, AssemblyAI is a good fit for this, especially if you want to build the pipeline yourself through an API. I didn't verify current pricing or newer features, so check those on their site.

**What it offers for customer calls**
- **Transcription with speaker labels.** Diarization separates the agent from the customer, which most call analysis depends on.
- **Audio intelligence features.** The AWS Marketplace listing describes summarization, sentiment analysis, content moderation, and PII redaction. PII redaction matters for call recordings.
- **LeMUR.** This is their framework for running LLMs over transcripts. You can ask custom questions, pull out action items, or return structured data such as call reason, objections, and next steps. In 2024 they added Claude 3 models to it.

**Strengths**
- It's one API for transcription and analysis, so you don't have to connect an ASR vendor to a separate LLM.
- You can write your own prompts, so the output can match your own categories, such as churn risk or compliance checks.
- Built-in redaction and sentiment save you from building those yourself.

**Caveats**
- **It's a developer API, not a finished product.** Tools like Gong or Observe.AI come with dashboards, coaching workflows, and CRM integrations. With AssemblyAI you build those yourself.
- **Costs can add up.** One 2026 review says LeMUR costs scale quickly at high volume. The pricing figures I found came from third-party sites and conflicted with each other, and some were 2024 snapshots.
- **Accuracy depends on your audio.** Phone-quality audio, heavy accents, and industry jargon can hurt transcripts. Test on a sample of your own calls.
- **Summary quality depends on your prompts.** You'll need to iterate on them.

**Bottom line:** It works well if you have engineering resources and want flexible, custom call insights. If you want a ready-made conversation-intelligence tool for sales or support teams, a dedicated product is probably faster. Either way, run 20–50 of your real calls through it and compare the transcripts and summaries with a few alternatives, such as Deepgram or Whisper-based setups, before you commit.

question: What is AssemblyAI and what is it known for?
answer:
AssemblyAI is an AI company that builds speech-to-text and speech understanding models, which developers use through an API. I'm answering from memory and haven't searched for recent news. Details like product names, model versions and pricing change often, so check their site for current information.

**What it does**
- **Speech-to-text (speech recognition):** It transcribes pre-recorded audio and video files. It also transcribes live audio in real time through streaming.
- **Audio intelligence:** It offers features built on top of transcripts, such as:
  - speaker diarization (who said what)
  - sentiment analysis
  - topic and entity detection
  - content moderation
  - PII redaction
  - summarization
  - auto chapters
- **LLM-based tools:** It offers ways to apply large language models to transcripts, such as asking questions about a recording or generating summaries. It has marketed this under names like LeMUR.

**What it's known for**
- **Developer-friendly API:** It's easy to integrate, has good documentation, and offers SDKs in several languages. Many startups and product teams use it to add transcription without building their own models.
- **Accuracy and its own models:** It trains its own speech models, including the Universal and Slam series. It competes on accuracy, multilingual support, and robustness to noisy audio and accents.
- **Competition:** Its main rivals are Deepgram, OpenAI Whisper, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, AWS Transcribe, and Rev.
- **Typical customers:** Companies building:
  - call-center and conversation-intelligence tools
  - meeting note-takers
  - podcast and video platforms
  - voice agents
  - media and captioning products
- **Company background:** It was founded in 2017 by Dylan Fox and is based in San Francisco. It has raised substantial venture funding from investors including Accel, Insight Partners, and Y Combinator.

I can search for its latest models, pricing, or how it compares with a specific competitor if you'd like.

question: Is AssemblyAI good for extracting insights and summaries from customer calls?
answer:
**Yes, AssemblyAI is a good fit for this, especially if you want one API for transcription and analysis.** Some pricing details below are unconfirmed.

**Strengths**
- **Transcription accuracy:** It offers speaker diarization and speaker identification, which matter for separating agent and customer. Accuracy on noisy phone audio is usually the biggest factor in downstream insight quality.
- **Built-in analysis:** Its Speech Understanding features include summarization, sentiment analysis, entity detection, topic and content classification, and translation. One usage-tracking page says Auto Chapters has been folded into Summarization, with effort-based tiers. I couldn't confirm that from AssemblyAI's own pages.
- **LLM Gateway:** You can run custom prompts over transcripts, such as "list objections raised", "was the issue resolved?" or "extract action items". It supports Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models. This is the most flexible route for call-specific insights, because you can define your own schema and scoring rubrics.
- **Developer experience:** Both pre-recorded and streaming modes are available, so you can do post-call analysis or live agent assist.

**Caveats**
- **No finished call-center product:** It is an API platform, not a conversation-intelligence tool like Gong, Observe.AI or CallRail. You build the dashboards, QA scorecards, CRM sync and trend reporting yourself.
- **Costs add up:** Transcription is billed per hour, add-ons are billed on top, and LLM Gateway is billed per token. Per the search results, base rates are about $0.15/hr for Universal-2 and $0.21/hr for Universal-3.5 Pro. Speaker Identification adds $0.02/hr and Translation adds $0.06/hr. I couldn't confirm summarization pricing, and the figures came from third-party aggregators. Check assemblyai.com/pricing before budgeting.
- **Compliance:** If your calls contain PII, PHI or payment data, check their PII redaction options, data retention settings and compliance certifications.

**Rule of thumb**
- **Choose AssemblyAI** if you have engineering resources and want custom insights or want to embed analysis in your own product.
- **Choose a packaged tool** if you want out-of-the-box coaching, scorecards and CRM integrations with no build effort.

I'd test it on 20–50 of your real calls. Compare transcript accuracy, especially on jargon, accents and crosstalk. Also check whether the summaries match what your team actually needs.

question: What is AssemblyAI and what is it known for?
answer:
AssemblyAI is an AI company that builds speech-to-text and speech understanding models, which it offers to developers through an API. I'm answering from memory and didn't search, so details such as current products and pricing may have changed.

**What it does**
- **Speech-to-text transcription:** It converts audio and video, both pre-recorded and real-time streaming, into text.
- **Audio intelligence features:** These include speaker diarization (who said what), sentiment analysis, entity detection, topic detection, auto chapters and summarization, content moderation, and PII redaction.
- **LLM-based features:** Its LeMUR framework (and later tools) lets developers apply large language models to transcripts, for example to summarize calls or answer questions about them.

**What it's known for**
- **Developer-friendly API:** Teams can add transcription and audio analysis to their products without building their own models.
- **Accuracy:** It has focused on high-accuracy speech recognition. Its Universal and Slam-1 models, and the earlier Conformer-based models, are examples.
- **Customers:** Companies building call-center analytics, meeting note-takers, podcast and media tools, and conversational intelligence products use it.
- **Funding and background:** It was founded in 2017 and is based in San Francisco. It has raised substantial venture funding from investors such as Accel, Insight Partners, and Y Combinator.

Competitors include Deepgram, OpenAI Whisper, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, AWS Transcribe, and Rev AI.

I can search for its latest models, pricing, or news if you'd like.

question: What is the best framework for building AI agents in Python?
answer:
There's no single best framework. The right choice depends on what you're building. This is my general knowledge, and I haven't checked what has changed recently.

**Good defaults**
- **Claude Agent SDK (Anthropic)**: Best if you want a production-grade agent loop with tool use, file and shell access, MCP support, subagents, and context management built in. It's a good fit for coding, research, and automation agents built on Claude.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK**: A lightweight option with few abstractions: agents, handoffs, guardrails, and tracing. Despite the name, it works with other model providers.
- **PydanticAI**: Type-safe and Pythonic, with structured outputs and validation. It's model-agnostic and a good fit if you like FastAPI-style ergonomics.

**For complex workflows**
- **LangGraph**: Models agents as stateful graphs. It handles branching, persistence, human-in-the-loop steps, and long-running or multi-step workflows. It has the largest ecosystem, but a steeper learning curve and more abstraction.
- **Google ADK**: A good choice if you're on Google Cloud or Gemini.

**For multi-agent setups**
- **CrewAI**: Role-based agent teams. It's quick to prototype, but less flexible for fine-grained control.
- **AutoGen / Microsoft Agent Framework**: Conversational multi-agent patterns, well suited to enterprise and Azure setups.

**For data and RAG-heavy agents**
- **LlamaIndex**: A strong choice when retrieval over your own documents is central.

**My rule of thumb**
1. Start with the simplest thing: a provider SDK plus a tool-calling loop. Many agents don't need a framework.
2. Use the Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, or PydanticAI when you want a thin, well-designed layer.
3. Use LangGraph when you need explicit control flow, checkpointing, or complex state.
4. Avoid heavy frameworks until you know you need what they offer. Heavy abstractions make debugging harder.

If you tell me your use case (model provider, single or multi-agent, production or prototype), I can narrow it down. I can also search for the latest comparisons, since this space changes fast.

question: What is the best framework for building AI agents in Python?
answer:
There's no single best framework. It depends on what you're building. This is my general knowledge, and I haven't checked it against current releases, so verify versions and features before you commit.

**Main options**

- **Claude Agent SDK (Anthropic)**: Good for coding, file, and tool-using agents. It gives you the same agent loop, tool handling, context management, MCP support, and subagents that Claude Code uses. It's a strong choice if you're using Claude and want a capable agent with little scaffolding.
- **LangGraph (LangChain)**: Good for complex, stateful workflows. It models agents as graphs, with persistence, human-in-the-loop steps, and streaming. It's widely used in production and has a large ecosystem and good observability through LangSmith. The drawback is a steeper learning curve and more abstraction.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK**: Lightweight, with a small set of primitives (agents, handoffs, guardrails, tracing). It's easy to learn, and it works with other providers.
- **Pydantic AI**: Type-safe and Pythonic, with structured outputs and validation. It suits teams that value clean code and reliability.
- **CrewAI**: Role-based multi-agent teams. It's fast for prototyping, but you get less control than with LangGraph.
- **AutoGen / Microsoft Agent Framework**: Multi-agent conversations, aimed at enterprise and Azure users.
- **LlamaIndex**: Best when your agent is centered on RAG and data over documents.
- **smolagents (Hugging Face)**: Minimal, with agents that write code as their actions. Good for open models and experiments.

**Quick recommendations**

- Simple agent with tool use, on Claude: **Claude Agent SDK**, or just the Anthropic API with a tool-use loop.
- Complex, durable, branching workflows: **LangGraph**.
- Type safety and structured outputs: **Pydantic AI**.
- Fast multi-agent prototype: **CrewAI** or the **OpenAI Agents SDK**.
- Document-heavy RAG agents: **LlamaIndex**.

**Advice**

Many production agents are just an LLM, a tool loop, and good prompts. Start with the raw API or a thin SDK, and add a heavier framework only when you need things like state persistence, retries, or multi-agent orchestration. Heavy abstractions can make debugging harder.

question: What is the best framework for building a RAG application?
answer:
There isn't one best framework. The right choice depends on what you're building. This is my general knowledge, not a fresh search, so check current versions before you commit.

**Main options**

- **LlamaIndex** is the most RAG-focused. It has strong document parsing, many data connectors, and flexible indexing and retrieval. It's a good default if retrieval quality over your documents is the core problem.
- **LangChain / LangGraph** is a general LLM orchestration framework with a huge ecosystem of integrations. LangGraph suits agentic or multi-step RAG with branching logic and state. It has more abstraction and API churn than the others.
- **Haystack (deepset)** uses explicit, typed pipelines. It's production-oriented and easy to test and reason about, which suits teams that want a clear architecture.
- **DSPy** treats prompts and retrieval steps as programs you can optimize automatically. It works well when you have evaluation data and want to tune quality systematically.
- **No framework (direct SDK, vector DB client, and your own code)** is often best for simple RAG. The core loop is small: chunk, embed, store, retrieve, (rerank), prompt. Fewer dependencies make debugging easier.

**Quick guidance**

| Situation | Pick |
|---|---|
| Prototype or document-heavy Q&A | LlamaIndex |
| Agents, tools, and complex workflows | LangGraph |
| Production pipelines with clear structure | Haystack |
| Optimizing quality against a metric | DSPy |
| Simple use case, or you want full control | Plain SDK and a vector DB |

**What matters more than the framework**

- Chunking strategy and document parsing quality
- Hybrid search (BM25 plus vectors) and a reranker
- An evaluation set, using tools like Ragas or your own test questions
- Metadata filtering and good embeddings

If you tell me your data type, scale, language (Python or TypeScript), and whether you need agents, I can give a more specific recommendation. I can also search for the latest comparisons.

- **LlamaIndex** is the strongest choice if retrieval is the core of your app. It has good data connectors, parsing, chunking, indexing, and query engines, and it's the most RAG-focused of the group.

**Lighter or more opinionated**
- **DSPy** treats prompts and retrieval as programs you can optimize. It's a good fit if you have eval data and want to tune systematically.
- **No framework**: a vector DB client, an embeddings API, and a direct LLM SDK call. For simple RAG this is often the most maintainable option, with fewer dependencies and abstractions to fight.

- Options include hosted file-search and retrieval tools from the model providers, AWS Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and Vertex AI Search. They're fast to ship but give you less control.

question: How do I build a stateful multi-agent workflow with human-in-the-loop steps?
answer:
The most common way to do this is with **LangGraph**. It gives you three things: shared state, checkpointing (persistence), and an `interrupt` primitive that pauses the graph for a human and resumes it later. I'm writing this from memory, so check the current docs for exact signatures.

## Core pieces

1. **State**: a typed schema that all agents read and write.
2. **Nodes**: each agent is a node, which is a function that takes state and returns updates.
3. **Checkpointer**: saves state after every step. Pausing and resuming depend on it. Use `InMemorySaver` for dev and Postgres or SQLite in production.
4. **`interrupt()` and `Command(resume=...)`**: the node pauses and surfaces a payload to the human. You resume the run with their response.
5. **`thread_id`**: identifies one workflow run, so you can resume the right one.

## Example

```python
from typing import TypedDict, Literal
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

class State(TypedDict):
    task: str
    draft: str
    approved: bool
    feedback: str

def researcher(state: State):
    return {"draft": f"Draft plan for: {state['task']}"}   # call your LLM/agent here

def human_review(state: State) -> Command[Literal["writer", "publisher"]]:
    decision = interrupt({
        "question": "Approve this draft?",
        "draft": state["draft"],
    })
    if decision["approved"]:
        return Command(goto="publisher", update={"approved": True})
    return Command(goto="writer", update={"feedback": decision["feedback"]})

def writer(state: State):
    return {"draft": state["draft"] + f"\n(revised: {state['feedback']})"}

def publisher(state: State):
    print("Publishing:", state["draft"])
    return {}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("researcher", researcher)
g.add_node("human_review", human_review)
g.add_node("writer", writer)
g.add_node("publisher", publisher)
g.add_edge(START, "researcher")
g.add_edge("researcher", "human_review")
g.add_edge("writer", "human_review")   # loop back for re-review
g.add_edge("publisher", END)

app = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "run-42"}}
result = app.invoke({"task": "Q4 launch"}, cfg)
print(result["__interrupt__"])          # shows the payload for the human

# ...later, possibly in another process if the checkpointer is durable...
app.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": False, "feedback": "add risks"}), cfg)
```

## Design tips

- **Interrupted nodes re-run from the start on resume.** Keep side effects (emails, API writes) out of the code before `interrupt()`, or make them idempotent.
- **Put approval gates before irreversible actions**, such as sending, paying, or deleting. You can also add them around risky tool calls.
- **Use a durable checkpointer** (Postgres or Redis) if humans may take hours or days to respond.
- **Handle multiple interrupts** by resuming with a map of interrupt IDs to values when agents run in parallel.
- **Expose it through an API.** `POST /runs` starts a run, `GET /runs/{id}` returns pending interrupts, and `POST /runs/{id}/resume` calls `Command(resume=...)`. Slack, a web UI, or email can all sit on top.
- **Multi-agent structure**: use a supervisor node that routes with `Command(goto=...)` to worker agents, or make each worker its own subgraph. Interrupts inside subgraphs propagate up to the parent.
- **Time travel and editing**: you can inspect or modify state with `app.get_state(cfg)` and `app.update_state(cfg, {...})` before resuming. This lets a human edit the draft directly instead of just approving it.

## Alternatives

- **Claude Agent SDK**: use permission callbacks or hooks for approval gates, and session resumption for persistence.
- **Temporal, Inngest, or Restate**: durable workflow engines. Use signals or events to wait for a human. They're better when you need long-running, reliable orchestration with agents as steps.
- **AutoGen, CrewAI, or OpenAI Agents SDK**: each has its own human-input or approval mechanism, but persistence is usually less built-in.

If you tell me which framework or language you're using, and whether approvals are quick (a chat prompt) or slow (hours or days), I can tailor this. I can also scaffold a working project in your directory.

question: How do I build a stateful multi-agent workflow with human-in-the-loop steps?
answer:
The most common approach is **LangGraph**. It gives you shared state, checkpointing (persistence), and a built-in pause/resume primitive for human input. The same pattern applies in other frameworks.

## Core concepts

1. **Shared state**: a typed object that every agent (node) reads from and writes to.
2. **Checkpointer**: saves state after each step, keyed by a `thread_id`. This lets a run pause for hours or days and resume later, even after a restart.
3. **Interrupt**: a node calls `interrupt(payload)`. The graph halts and surfaces the payload to your app. You resume it with `Command(resume=value)`.
4. **Routing**: conditional edges or `Command(goto=...)` send control between agents based on state and human decisions.

## Example

```python
from typing import TypedDict, Literal
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver  # use PostgresSaver/SqliteSaver in prod

class State(TypedDict):
    task: str
    draft: str
    feedback: str
    approved: bool

def writer(state: State):
    # call your LLM/agent here
    draft = f"Draft for: {state['task']}. Feedback: {state.get('feedback','')}"
    return {"draft": draft}

def human_review(state: State) -> Command[Literal["writer", "publisher"]]:
    decision = interrupt({
        "question": "Approve this draft?",
        "draft": state["draft"],
    })
    if decision["approved"]:
        return Command(goto="publisher", update={"approved": True})
    return Command(goto="writer", update={"feedback": decision["feedback"]})

def publisher(state: State):
    print("Publishing:", state["draft"])
    return {}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("writer", writer)
g.add_node("human_review", human_review)
g.add_node("publisher", publisher)
g.add_edge(START, "writer")
g.add_edge("writer", "human_review")
g.add_edge("publisher", END)

app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "job-42"}}

# Run until the interrupt
result = app.invoke({"task": "Announce v2 release"}, cfg)
print(result["__interrupt__"])   # payload shown to the human

# Later, possibly from a different process/request: resume with the human's input
app.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": False, "feedback": "Shorter, please"}), cfg)
app.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": True}), cfg)
```

## Multi-agent structure

- Make each agent a node, or a subgraph with its own tools. Examples are researcher, writer, and reviewer.
- Add a **supervisor** node that uses `Command(goto=...)` to pick the next agent, or use direct edges for a fixed pipeline.
- Put human checkpoints where actions are risky or irreversible, such as sending email, spending money, or writing to production. You can also put them where the model's confidence is low.

## Practical tips

- **Code before `interrupt()` re-runs on resume.** The node restarts from the top, so keep side effects after the interrupt or make them idempotent.
- **Use a durable checkpointer in production** (Postgres, SQLite, or Redis). `MemorySaver` is lost on restart.
- **Expose the pause through your API or UI.** Store `thread_id`, show the interrupt payload (for example in Slack, a web form, or a ticket), and call resume when the human responds.
- **Human actions can include more than approve or reject.** Editing state directly, redirecting to another agent, and supplying missing info all work. You can also edit state out-of-band with `app.update_state(cfg, {...})`.
- **Add timeouts or escalation** outside the graph. A scheduler can resume with a default or notify someone if no one responds.
- **Review a tool call before it runs.** Put the `interrupt()` inside the tool wrapper, or in a node just before the tool node.
- **Debug with time travel.** Checkpoints let you inspect history and replay from earlier states.

## Alternatives

- **Temporal / Inngest / Restate**: durable workflow engines with signals or "wait for event" steps. They're good if you need strong reliability guarantees, with agents as activities.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, AutoGen/AG2**: each has its own human-input or approval hooks. Persistence is usually less built-in, so you may need to add your own.
- **Claude Agent SDK**: use permission callbacks and hooks to pause for approval on tool use, with session resume for state.

1. **Shared state**: a typed object that every agent (node) reads from and writes to.
2. **Checkpointer**: saves state after each step, keyed by a `thread_id`. This lets a run pause for hours or days and resume later, even after a restart.
3. **Interrupt**: a node calls `interrupt(payload)`. The graph halts and surfaces the payload to your app. You resume it with `Command(resume=value)`.
4. **Routing**: conditional edges or `Command(goto=...)` send control between agents based on state and human decisions.

## Example

```python
from typing import TypedDict, Literal
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver  # use PostgresSaver/SqliteSaver in prod

class State(TypedDict):
    task: str
    draft: str
    feedback: str
    approved: bool

def writer(state: State):
    # call your LLM/agent here
    draft = f"Draft for: {state['task']}. Feedback: {state.get('feedback','')}"
    return {"draft": draft}

def human_review(state: State) -> Command[Literal["writer", "publisher"]]:
    decision = interrupt({
        "question": "Approve this draft?",
        "draft": state["draft"],
    })
    if decision["approved"]:
        return Command(goto="publisher", update={"approved": True})
    return Command(goto="writer", update={"feedback": decision["feedback"]})

def publisher(state: State):
    print("Publishing:", state["draft"])
    return {}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("writer", writer)
g.add_node("human_review", human_review)
g.add_node("publisher", publisher)
g.add_edge(START, "writer")
g.add_edge("writer", "human_review")
g.add_edge("publisher", END)

app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "job-42"}}

# Run until the interrupt
result = app.invoke({"task": "Announce v2 release"}, cfg)
print(result["__interrupt__"])   # payload shown to the human

# Later, possibly from a different process/request: resume with the human's input
app.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": False, "feedback": "Shorter, please"}), cfg)
app.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": True}), cfg)
```

## Multi-agent structure

- Make each agent a node, or a subgraph with its own tools. Examples are researcher, writer, and reviewer.
- Add a **supervisor** node that uses `Command(goto=...)` to pick the next agent, or use direct edges for a fixed pipeline.
- Put human checkpoints where actions are risky or irreversible, such as sending email, spending money, or writing to production. You can also put them where the model's confidence is low.

## Practical tips

- **Code before `interrupt()` re-runs on resume.** The node restarts from the top, so keep side effects after the interrupt or make them idempotent.
- **Use a durable checkpointer in production** (Postgres, SQLite, or Redis). `MemorySaver` is lost on restart.
- **Expose the pause through your API or UI.** Store `thread_id`, show the interrupt payload (for example in Slack, a web form, or a ticket), and call resume when the human responds.
- **Human actions can include more than approve or reject.** Editing state directly, redirecting to another agent, and supplying missing info all work. You can also edit state out-of-band with `app.update_state(cfg, {...})`.
- **Add timeouts or escalation** outside the graph. A scheduler can resume with a default or notify someone if no one responds.
- **Review a tool call before it runs.** Put the `interrupt()` inside the tool wrapper, or in a node just before the tool node.
- **Debug with time travel.** Checkpoints let you inspect history and replay from earlier states.

## Alternatives

- **Temporal / Inngest / Restate**: durable workflow engines with signals or "wait for event" steps. They're good if you need strong reliability guarantees, with agents as activities.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, AutoGen/AG2**: each has its own human-input or approval hooks. Persistence is usually less built-in, so you may need to add your own.
- **Claude Agent SDK**: use permission callbacks and hooks to pause for approval on tool use, with session resume for state.

I can adapt this to a specific framework, or to a use case such as approval gates, a supervisor with several specialist agents, or a Slack/web UI integration. Which do you want?

question: What is the best tool for LLM observability and evaluation?
answer:
There isn't one best tool. The right choice depends on your stack and constraints. This is from my background knowledge, and I haven't searched for anything newer, so check current features and pricing before you commit.

**Strong general-purpose options**
- **Langfuse** is open source and self-hostable. It covers tracing, prompt management, datasets, and evals. It's a good default if you want control over your data and no vendor lock-in.
- **LangSmith** is the best fit if you use LangChain or LangGraph. Its tracing, datasets, and eval workflows are polished. It's a hosted product, with self-hosting only on enterprise plans.
- **Arize Phoenix** is open source and built on OpenTelemetry/OpenInference. It's good for experimentation and RAG debugging. Arize AX is the commercial version.
- **Braintrust** has an eval-first workflow, with good experiment comparison and CI integration. It's popular with teams that treat evals like tests.

**Other options**
- **Weights & Biases Weave** suits teams already using W&B.
- **Helicone** is a proxy-based option that's quick to set up and strong on cost and latency monitoring.
- **Datadog LLM Observability** makes sense if you already use Datadog for everything else.
- **OpenTelemetry-based setups** (OpenLLMetry, OpenInference) avoid lock-in. You can send traces to any backend.

**Eval libraries** (these are often used alongside the platforms above)
- **DeepEval**, **Ragas** (RAG metrics), **promptfoo** (CLI and CI-friendly, also good for red-teaming), and **OpenAI Evals**.

**Quick picks**
- Open source and self-hosted: **Langfuse** or **Phoenix**
- LangChain/LangGraph stack: **LangSmith**
- Eval-driven development with CI: **Braintrust** or **promptfoo**
- Existing enterprise monitoring: **Datadog**

The tools in this space change quickly, and some have been acquired or have changed their pricing. If you tell me your framework, scale, and whether you need self-hosting, I can narrow it down. I can also search for current comparisons if you want.

question: What is the best TypeScript framework for building AI agents?
answer:
There's no single best one. It depends on what you're building. These are the main options:

**Top picks**
- **Vercel AI SDK**: The default for most TypeScript projects. It has a clean API, streaming, tool calling, structured output, and works with many model providers. It also has good React/Next.js integration and built-in agent loops. Choose it if you want a lightweight, flexible foundation without much lock-in.
- **Mastra**: A full TypeScript-first agent framework built on the AI SDK. It adds workflows, memory, RAG, evals, and observability. Choose it if you want batteries included.
- **Claude Agent SDK** (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`): The same agent harness that powers Claude Code. It comes with file, shell, and search tools, subagents, MCP, and context management. Choose it for coding or computer-use style agents built on Claude.

**Other strong options**
- **LangGraph.js**: Graph-based stateful workflows with checkpointing and human-in-the-loop. It suits complex, long-running orchestration, though it has a steeper learning curve.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK (JS/TS)**: Handoffs, guardrails, and tracing. It's a good fit if you're mostly on OpenAI models.
- **VoltAgent, Genkit (Google), and LlamaIndex.TS**: Worth a look for specific needs. VoltAgent is a TS-native agent framework with observability, Genkit works well in Google/Firebase stacks, and LlamaIndex.TS is strong for RAG-heavy work.

**Quick guide**
| Need | Pick |
|---|---|
| Simple chat or tool-using app, web UI | Vercel AI SDK |
| Full agent app with memory and workflows | Mastra |
| Autonomous coding or file/system agents | Claude Agent SDK |
| Complex stateful multi-step graphs | LangGraph.js |

My suggestion is to start with the Vercel AI SDK, or Mastra if you want more structure. Frameworks in this space change fast, and I haven't checked their current state. If you tell me your use case, model provider, and deployment target, I can narrow it down or look up the latest versions and features.

question: What is the best open-source agent framework for production use?
answer:
There isn't one best framework. It depends on your stack and how much control you need. I haven't searched for anything newer, and this space changes fast, so check release notes before you commit.

**Common production choices**

| Framework | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **LangGraph** (LangChain) | Complex, stateful, long-running workflows | It models agents as explicit graphs, with checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, and durable execution. It's probably the most widely deployed, and it integrates with LangSmith for observability. |
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | Simple, lightweight agents and handoffs | It has few abstractions, built-in tracing and guardrails, and supports non-OpenAI models. |
| **Claude Agent SDK** | Coding, computer-use, and tool-heavy agents | It's the same agent loop that powers Claude Code. It includes MCP support, subagents, and permissions. |
| **Pydantic AI** | Type-safe Python teams | It has strong validation, a clean API, and a FastAPI-like developer experience. |
| **Google ADK** | GCP/Vertex shops and multi-agent systems | It has good deployment tooling and supports A2A. |
| **Microsoft Agent Framework** (successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel) | .NET/Azure enterprises | It supports both Python and .NET. |
| **CrewAI** | Fast prototyping of role-based multi-agent setups | It's easy to start with, but you get less control when debugging at scale. |

**My default recommendation**
- **LangGraph** if you need reliability, state persistence, retries, and auditability. It's the most battle-tested for complex workflows.

question: LangChain vs LlamaIndex
answer:
# LangChain vs LlamaIndex

This comes from my general knowledge, not a fresh search. Both projects change quickly, so check the current docs for specifics.

## Core focus
- **LangChain** is a general framework for building LLM applications. It covers chains, tool use, agents, memory, and integrations. **LangGraph**, its sibling library, handles stateful, multi-step agent workflows. **LangSmith** handles tracing and evaluation.
- **LlamaIndex** centers on data and retrieval: ingesting, indexing, and querying your own data (RAG). It has also added agent and workflow features.

## Strengths
| | LangChain | LlamaIndex |
|---|---|---|
| **RAG** | Workable, but you assemble more of it yourself | Best-in-class abstractions: loaders, node parsers, indices, retrievers, query engines, rerankers |
| **Agents / orchestration** | Strong, especially with LangGraph (branching, loops, human-in-the-loop, persistence) | Capable (Workflows, agent classes), but less mature for complex control flow |
| **Integrations** | Very large ecosystem (models, vector stores, tools) | Large, with a focus on data connectors (LlamaHub) |
| **Document parsing** | Basic loaders | LlamaParse and strong handling of complex documents |
| **Observability** | LangSmith | Integrates with several tools (Arize, Langfuse, etc.) |

## When to choose which
- **Choose LlamaIndex if** your main problem is "chat with my documents." That includes complex PDFs, many data sources, and tuning retrieval quality.
- **Choose LangChain/LangGraph if** you're building agents or multi-step workflows with tools, branching logic, and state. It also fits if you want a broad ecosystem and tracing tooling.
- **Use both** if it suits you. Many teams use LlamaIndex for retrieval and LangChain/LangGraph for orchestration.

## Caveats
- The two have converged: each now covers part of the other's territory.
- LangChain has been criticized for abstraction overhead and API churn. Recent versions have narrowed the core API and moved many integrations into separate packages.
- For simple use cases, calling the model provider's SDK directly plus a vector DB client may be simpler than either framework.

If you tell me your use case (RAG over PDFs, agents, a production chatbot, etc.), I can give a more specific recommendation. I can also search for the latest versions and features.

question: LangGraph vs CrewAI for multi-agent systems
answer:
# LangGraph vs CrewAI

I answered this from background knowledge without searching, so check version-specific details against the current docs.

## Core difference
- **LangGraph** is a low-level orchestration framework. You model your system as a **graph**: nodes are functions or agents, edges are control flow, and shared state is explicit. You control exactly what runs and when.
- **CrewAI** is a higher-level, **role-based** framework. You define agents (role, goal, backstory), tasks, and a "crew" that runs them. It also offers **Flows** for more deterministic, event-driven orchestration.

## Comparison

| | LangGraph | CrewAI |
|---|---|---|
| Abstraction | Low-level graph and state machine | High-level roles, tasks, crews |
| Learning curve | Steeper | Gentler, quick to prototype |
| Control flow | Explicit: branches, loops, cycles, conditional edges | Mostly sequential or hierarchical, with Flows for finer control |
| State management | First-class typed state and reducers, with checkpointing | Simpler, mostly passing task outputs and context |
| Human-in-the-loop | Strong: interrupts, pause/resume, time-travel debugging | Supported, but less granular |
| Persistence and durability | Built-in checkpointers, resumable runs | More limited |
| Observability | LangSmith integration, streaming of intermediate steps | Built-in tracing and enterprise tooling, plus third-party integrations |
| Ecosystem | LangChain ecosystem, though usable standalone | Independent, with its own tools and a growing enterprise platform |
| Best for | Complex, long-running, production-critical workflows | Fast prototyping, clear role-based pipelines |

## When to choose which

**Choose LangGraph if:**
- You need fine-grained control over branching, retries, loops, or error handling.
- Runs are long and must be resumable or recoverable after failures.
- You need human approval steps, auditability, or time-travel debugging.
- You're building production systems where predictability matters.

**Choose CrewAI if:**
- You want a working multi-agent prototype fast.
- Your problem maps naturally to a team of specialists, such as researcher, writer, and reviewer.
- You prefer readable, declarative configuration (YAML for agents and tasks).
- Your team is less comfortable with graph or state-machine thinking.

## Tradeoffs to know
- **CrewAI** can feel opaque when agents behave unexpectedly, because the abstraction hides the prompts and control flow. Debugging and customization can get harder as complexity grows.
- **LangGraph** needs more boilerplate and upfront design. That is the cost of its control.
- Many teams prototype in CrewAI and move to LangGraph when they need more reliability. Others stay in CrewAI, especially with Flows.

## Rule of thumb
Use **CrewAI** to explore an idea quickly. Use **LangGraph** when you need to guarantee how the system behaves in production.

If you tell me your use case (for example research automation, customer support, or code generation), your scale, and your team's experience, I can recommend one. I can also look up the latest releases and features for both.

question: What is the best TypeScript framework for building AI agents?
answer:
There isn't one best framework. The right choice depends on what you're building. These are the main options, and I haven't checked them against anything released recently:

**Top picks**
- **Vercel AI SDK**: The best default for most TypeScript developers. It's lightweight and provider-agnostic, with strong streaming, tool calling, structured output, and multi-step agent loops. It fits well with Next.js and React UIs.
- **Mastra**: A full TypeScript-first agent framework. It includes agents, workflows, RAG, memory, evals, and observability. It's a good choice if you want batteries included without moving to Python.
- **LangGraph.js**: Best for complex, stateful, graph-based workflows. It has human-in-the-loop support, persistence, and branching control flow. It's more verbose and has a steeper learning curve.

**Provider-specific SDKs**
- **Claude Agent SDK** (Anthropic): Gives you the same agent loop, tools, and context management that Claude Code uses. It's a good fit for coding or file/computer-oriented agents on Claude.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK (JS/TS)**: Has a simple model of agents, handoffs, and guardrails. It's best if you're mostly on OpenAI models.

**Others worth knowing**
- **LlamaIndex.TS**: Strong when RAG and data ingestion are central.
- **VoltAgent, Genkit (Google), and Inngest AgentKit**: Good for specific needs. Genkit suits Google and Firebase stacks. AgentKit suits durable, event-driven execution.

**Rule of thumb**
- Web app with an AI chat or agent UI: Vercel AI SDK.
- A full agent platform in TypeScript: Mastra.
- Complex stateful orchestration: LangGraph.js.
- Mostly one model vendor: that vendor's SDK.
- A simple agent: skip the framework and write a tool-calling loop around a provider SDK. It's often under 100 lines and easier to debug.

If you tell me your use case (model provider, UI or backend, and how complex the workflows are), I can narrow it to one choice. I can also search for the latest comparisons, since this space changes quickly.
